attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own Substack post.

semantics.note: A faithful present-tense observation listing five abilities, dated to the post by 'as of today'.

contract.note: Reading 'pretty poor' as clearly below typical humans, and requiring all five abilities for full support, is a fair ordinary reading. The 2023 window is reasonable. The result depends on reading thresholds and benchmarks that Marcus never named.

evidence.note: GPT-4 scored 33% on ConceptARC against about 91% for humans, in Nov 2023. This supports the cognitive-flexibility item only.
GPT-4V failed simple abstract grid tasks. These are not natural scenes, so the result bears only loosely on scene comprehension.

A company disclosure about scores on professional exams. These are not tests built to measure inferring semantics, and OpenAI also concedes GPT-4 is less capable than humans in many real-world settings.

reviews.rationale: Only cognitive flexibility is clearly backed by an independent human-vs-AI test. The packet has no 2023 comparisons for world models, 3D navigation or natural-scene comprehension, and for semantics it offers only a company's exam claims. The contract needs all five abilities for support and most of them for contradiction, so the evidence settles neither.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own Substack post.

semantics.note: Faithful. It keeps the examples and the 'unusual situations' qualifier on planning.

contract.note: Reading 'machines' as the best 2023 computers and AI, and 'way behind' as well below humans on tests of novel abstraction and planning, is a fair, ordinary reading of rhetorical but firm language.

evidence.note: The Nov 2023 TOP500 list shows Frontier at about 1.19 EFlop/s, vastly beyond any human rate of floating point arithmetic.
On ConceptARC (2023), humans scored 91%, the best program 52% and GPT-4 25%. This is a large gap in flexible abstraction.
With better prompting in Nov 2023, GPT-4 still reached only 33%, well below humans.
In this NeurIPS 2023 study, GPT-4 produced executable plans only about 12% of the time. There is no human baseline in the excerpt, so the gap to humans is inferred.

reviews.rationale: Machine floating point throughput clearly holds. Independent 2023 tests show leading AI far below humans on flexible abstraction. On planning, autonomous success by the best LLM was low, though the human comparison is inferred rather than measured. Nothing in the packet shows AI at or near human level on these tasks.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own Substack post.

semantics.note: 'Almost certainly' signals high confidence, so this is a scorable claim about how AGI will be built. The drafter's modality 'likely' understates it. It is best treated as an open-horizon forecast, as the contract does.

contract.note: Settling the claim on the design of the first widely recognised AGI is fair. However, the AGI definition and the loose word 'disparate' leave the result open to interpretation.

reviews.rationale: No deadline was stated. The packet finds no system widely recognised as AGI by the evaluation date, so the early-resolution event has not happened. Absence of AGI is not failure, and the forecast stays open.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own Substack post.

semantics.note: A faithful general claim that world models are a necessary condition for reliable reasoning, keeping 'no matter how much memory or compute'.

contract.note: The contract rightly treats the claim as untestable: there is no operational definition of world models or of reliable reasoning, and the claim has universal scope over compute.

reviews.rationale: This is a theoretical necessary-condition claim with no agreed test for its key terms. No finite set of experiments can confirm 'regardless of compute', and refuting it would first need agreement that some system lacks world models. So it cannot be scored.
